extracted.intended_audience: AIPLA members, IP practitioners, law firm and corporate IP administrators, and researchers who use or interpret the AIPLA Economic Survey data
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and survey-design conventions, definitions, and question-wording changes used in the AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey 2023 to collect and present data about IP practitioners (income, billing, practice, budgets, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of 'design' as a technical specialization category
rubrics_metrics.description: Design was added as a category for the technical specialization time spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting time devoted to technical specializations, include 'design' as a possible category alongside mechanical, software, chemical, electrical, biotechnology, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing mediation cost question
rubrics_metrics.description: The litigation line item related to mediation was rephrased from 'cost of mediation' (2021) to 'cost if dispute was resolved through mediation' (2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the updated wording when asking or interpreting mediation-related litigation cost responses to clarify the scenario being priced (resolution via mediation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of COVID-19 references and rephrasing of remote-work/office/summer associate items
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the COVID-19 pandemic were removed from the 2023 Firm Survey and questions related to remote work, office space and summer associates were rephrased and/or expanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use pandemic-specific wording; interpret remote-work and office-space questions according to the new, generalized wording in the 2023 instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm respondent solo-practitioner and expanded demographic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm respondents were asked if they were a solo practitioner, and the gender and ethnicity questions were expanded to include detail related to the specific positions held by professionals who primarily practice IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey collection distinguishes solo practitioners at the firm level and collects more granular gender/ethnicity information tied to job position.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage in services-outsourced question and new service categories
rubrics_metrics.description: For services outsourced, responding law firms were asked if artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used when the service was not outsourced. Litigation services was also added as a service category for this question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting outsourced services, include whether in-house AI tools were used for the service and include litigation as an explicit category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Added promotion and paralegal salary questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A question asking firm respondents to report the number of associates promoted in 2022 to non-equity partner and equity partner was added along with a question that asks for the average salary for an IP paralegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect promotion counts by promotion type and capture average paralegal salary as a distinct data item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Added privacy/cybersecurity billing and cyber-liability insurance items
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy/cybersecurity was added as a line item to the question regarding the firm's 2022 IP billings, and two questions were incorporated into the survey to address cyber liability insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include privacy/cybersecurity in IP billing breakdowns and collect cyber-liability insurance information through the added questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing section replaced with detailed billable-hour credit items
rubrics_metrics.description: The Marketing section of the firm survey was removed and replaced with an expanded and more detailed question regarding associates' 'billable hour' credit toward their billing requirement for time spent performing various activities. Activities were listed separately (previously grouped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect billable-hour credit for individual activities separately; newly added activity categories include pro bono work, RFP process, and newsletter drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 10th and 90th percentiles from some tables
rubrics_metrics.description: The 10th and 90th percentiles were removed from various tables run for the Individual Survey due to high variability combined with low counts in some categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not display 10th/90th percentile columns in affected tables; rely on other distributional measures (quartiles, median) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-time only display for 2022 gross income and 2023 expected gross income
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables displaying the 2022 gross income and 2023 expected gross income only include full-time respondents in 2023; summary tables for part-time respondents have been added in the appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing income tables across years, note that 2022/2023 displayed income tables in this report use full-time respondents only; check appendix for part-time summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum responses required to show mean and median values
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimum of three responses is required to show mean and median values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fewer than three responses are available for a table cell or subgroup, suppress the mean and median and use the 'ISD' or omit the row, per anonymity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISD label for insufficient data and omission for small counts
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'ISD' is used to show insufficient data. Table rows with one or two respondents have been omitted to protect the anonymity of respondents, and tables with no valid rows have likewise been omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 'ISD' or remove rows/tables to prevent disclosure when counts are too small (1–2 respondents) or when no valid data exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: tables with less than 20 respondents generally not shown
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, tables with less than 20 respondents overall were not shown in order to maintain statistical reliability of the data; however, exceptions were made, and some tables were included despite having fewer than 20 respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 20 respondents as the target minimum for showing a table; document exceptions where tables with <20 respondents are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location table suppression rule for typical charges and litigation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Location tables that display data for typical charges and litigation related matters were deleted when there were less than 20 respondents. The corresponding charges and litigation tables with data displayed by number of attorneys were kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For location-specific typical charges/litigation tables require ≥20 respondents; alternative breakouts (by number of attorneys) may be retained even if location breakouts are suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartiles definition (first, median, third)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartiles are used to show distributions of real numbers. Responses are described by three quartiles: the first quartile, the median, and the third quartile. Quartiles identify interpolated locations on a distribution of values and do not necessarily represent actual reported values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand quartiles as the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles; values may be interpolated and need not correspond to an actual respondent value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Median definition and display thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The median identifies the point in the distribution of reported values that is equal to or larger than one-half of reported values and equal to or smaller than one-half—that is, the mid-point. A median is shown when three or more values were reported by respondents. The first and third quartiles are shown when four or more values were reported by respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show medians only for N≥3 and show first/third quartiles only for N≥4; treat reported quartiles/medians as estimates of the population distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean definition and display threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean is shown when three or more values were reported by respondents. It is equal to the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the arithmetic mean only for N≥3; note that the mean can exceed the median due to high-value outliers and small sample effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentages rounding note
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentages in some tables and graphs may not sum exactly due to rounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect minor rounding discrepancies when summing percentage columns; include a note explaining this to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Income: Defined as 'total gross income in calendar year 2022 from your primary practice…including any partnership income, cash bonus, share of profits, and similar income you received, and any deferred compensation in which you vested in 2022.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collecting or interpreting reported income, include all listed components (salary, partnership income, cash bonus, profit share, and vested deferred compensation) for the calendar year specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical Charges: respondent instructions and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical Charges: Respondents were instructed to respond 'only if you have been personally responsible for a representative sample of the type of work to which the question pertains, either as a service provider (i.e., an attorney in private practice) or as a purchaser of such services (i.e., corporate counsel).' Respondents were directed to assume 'a typical case with no unusual complications,' and were asked 'what did you charge (or would have charged, e.g., based on a fixed fee rate schedule) or what were you charged (or would have expected to be charged, e.g., based on a fixed fee rate schedule), in 2022, for legal services only (including search fees, but not including copy costs, drawing fees or government fees) in each of the following types of US matters?' Respondents were also asked to indicate the type of fee primarily used in 2022 (i.e., fixed fee, hourly, other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only respondents with personal responsibility for representative cases should answer; use 'typical' case assumptions; include legal-services-only costs (include search fees; exclude copy, drawing, government fees) and report primary fee type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated Litigation Costs: scope and 'total cost' components
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated Litigation Costs: Respondents were instructed to respond 'only if you have personal knowledge either as a service provider (attorney in private practice) or as a purchaser of such services (corporate counsel) of the costs incurred within the relatively recent past, for the type of work to which the question pertains.' In each of the questions, 'total cost' is all costs, including outside legal and paralegal services, local counsel, associates, paralegals, travel and living expenses, fees and costs for court reporters, photocopies, courier services, exhibit preparation, analytical testing, expert witnesses, translators, surveys, jury advisors, and similar expenses. Respondents were further instructed to estimate these based on a single IP asset, such as one patent at issue or one trademark, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only respondents with relevant personal knowledge should estimate litigation costs; include the comprehensive list of 'total cost' components and base estimates on a single IP asset for comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location definitions and metropolitan grouping rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Location: The metropolitan areas of Boston, New York City, Philadelphia, Washington (DC-MD-VA), Chicago, and Minneapolis–St. Paul include all localities—central city and surrounding areas—within the primary metropolitan statistical area. Texas is the one state reported separately. There were sufficient responses to breakout Los Angeles and San Francisco separately; California firms outside of those metro areas were included in 'Other West.' Other categories exclude those named metropolitan areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CMSA/PMSA definitions when grouping respondents by location; report certain large metros separately and aggregate others into regional categories like 'Other West' or 'Other Central.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent primary practice categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents are categorized by primary practice into groups such as Private Firm (Solo Practitioner; Private Firm, Equity Partner; Private Firm, Partner-Track Attorney; Private Firm, Non-Partner Track Attorney; Private Firm, Agent; Private Firm, Of Counsel), Corporate (Corporate IP, Head; Corporate IP, Attorney; Corporate IP, Agent; Corporate Legal, Head; Corporate Legal, Attorney; Corporate Legal, Agent), PTO Examiner, PTO Admin/Management, Government IP (not PTO), and Other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify respondents according to these explicit practice-role categories for subgroup analysis and table breakouts.
